lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Structure of a Mammalian Tooth

pages.body:
Run your tongue over your teeth. Some feel sharp and thin while others feel broad and bumpy. Each tooth is held so firmly in the jaw that you can bite a piece of sugar cane without the tooth moving.

- Which part of a tooth can you see when you look in a mirror?
- What do you think holds a tooth so firmly in the jaw?

Mammals such as humans, goats, dogs and cattle have teeth fixed in sockets in the jawbones. In this lesson we study the three regions of a tooth and the layers inside it, and we link each part to the work it does.

We begin with the regions of a tooth that can be seen from the outside.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The three regions of a tooth

pages.title: The three regions of a tooth
pages.body:
| **Region** | **Where it is found** | **Function** |
|---|---|---|
| Crown | The part above the gum that can be seen in the mouth | Bites, cuts, tears or grinds food |
| Neck | The narrow part at the gum line, between the crown and the root | Joins the crown to the root and is gripped by the gum |
| Root | The part below the gum, hidden in a socket in the jawbone | Holds the tooth firmly in the jaw |

Next we cut through a tooth in our minds to see the layers from the outside to the centre.

questions.q: The part of a tooth that is seen above the gum is the

pages.title: The layers inside a tooth
pages.body:
| **Part** | **Description** | **Function** |
|---|---|---|
| Enamel | A white outer layer that covers the crown. It is the hardest substance in the human body and has no nerves | Protects the tooth from wear and gives a hard surface for biting and chewing |
| Dentine | A hard, yellowish, bone like layer beneath the enamel. It forms most of the tooth and contains tiny channels | Supports the enamel and passes feelings such as heat, cold and pain to the pulp |
| Pulp cavity | The soft centre of the tooth, which contains blood vessels and nerves | Blood vessels bring food and oxygen to keep the tooth alive, and nerves make the tooth sensitive |
| Cement | A thin, bone like layer that covers the root | Fixes the root to the fibres that hold the tooth in its socket |
| Gum | The soft pink tissue that covers the jawbone around the neck of the tooth | Protects the root and the jawbone and helps to hold the tooth in place |
| Jawbone | The bone with sockets in which the roots sit | Anchors the teeth |
[[pic: Vertical section through a molar tooth showing the crown, neck and root, with the enamel, dentine, pulp cavity with blood vessels and nerves, cement, gum and jawbone labelled.]]

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Two sets of teeth in a lifetime

pages.body:
Enamel cannot repair itself once it is damaged because it contains no living cells. This is why a hole in the enamel never heals on its own and must be filled by a dentist. Pain is felt only when the damage reaches the dentine or the pulp, where the nerves are.

Finally we see that humans grow two sets of teeth.

pages.title: Two sets of teeth in a lifetime
pages.body:
A child grows a first set of 20 teeth called milk teeth. They begin to appear at about six months of age. From about six years of age the milk teeth fall out one after another and are replaced by the permanent teeth. A full adult set has 32 permanent teeth, 16 in the upper jaw and 16 in the lower jaw. The last four molars, called wisdom teeth, usually appear between the ages of 17 and 25. A permanent tooth that is lost is never replaced naturally.

> **Did you know?** Tooth enamel is harder than bone, yet acids made by bacteria in the mouth can slowly dissolve it.

questions.q: How many permanent teeth does an adult human have?

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Types of Teeth and Their Functions

pages.body:
Think about eating a mango, a piece of grilled meat and a handful of roasted groundnuts. You do not use the same teeth for all three. You bite the mango with your front teeth, pull at the meat with the pointed teeth and crush the groundnuts with the back teeth.

- Why do you think the teeth at the front and the back of your mouth have different shapes?
- Which teeth would a dog use most when eating meat?

Humans have four types of teeth. Each type has a shape that suits its work. In this lesson we describe each type, state its function and count how many of each an adult has.

We start with the shape, position and work of each type.

pages.title: The four types of teeth
pages.body:
| **Type of tooth** | **Shape and position** | **Function** | **Number in an adult** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incisors | Flat with a sharp, chisel shaped edge and one root. They are at the front of the mouth | Biting and cutting food | 8 |
| Canines | Pointed and cone shaped with one long root. They are next to the incisors | Tearing and gripping food | 4 |
| Premolars | Broad with two points called cusps and one or two roots. They are behind the canines | Crushing and grinding food | 8 |
| Molars | Large and broad with four or five cusps and two or three roots. They are at the back of the mouth | Grinding and chewing food into small pieces | 12 |

[[pic: Side by side drawings of an incisor, a canine, a premolar and a molar showing the shape of the crown and the number of roots of each.]]

Now we count the teeth in each half of each jaw.

questions.q: The teeth used for tearing food are the
questions.e: Flesh eating mammals such as dogs and cats have long, sharp canines for holding and tearing meat.

pages.title: The arrangement of the teeth
pages.body:
In an adult each half of each jaw has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars, which is 8 teeth. There are four such halves, so the total is 8 multiplied by 4, which is 32 teeth. Scientists write this arrangement as a dental formula. For an adult human it is incisors 2 over 2, canines 1 over 1, premolars 2 over 2 and molars 3 over 3. The milk set has no premolars. Each half of a jaw in a child has 2 incisors, 1 canine and 2 molars, which gives 20 teeth.

Finally we link the teeth of an animal to the food it eats.

questions.q: How many molars are there in a full set of adult teeth?

pages.title: Teeth and diet
pages.body:
- Flesh eating mammals such as dogs and cats have long, sharp canines for holding and tearing meat.
- Plant eating mammals such as cattle, goats and sheep have broad, flat molars for grinding grass. Cattle have no upper incisors and cut grass against a hard pad.
- Humans eat both plants and animals, so human teeth include all four types and none is very large.

Chewing breaks food into small pieces and mixes it with saliva. Small pieces are easier to swallow and give digestive enzymes a larger surface to work on. This is the link between the teeth and the digestion you studied in Basic 7.
> **Did you know?** The tusks of an elephant are incisors that never stop growing, and the long front teeth of a grasscutter also grow throughout its life.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Tooth Decay, Gum Disease and Care of the Teeth

pages.body:
Kofi loves toffees and sweet drinks and often goes to bed without cleaning his teeth. One morning he wakes up with a sharp pain in a back tooth, and his friend notices a brown hole in it.

- What do you think caused the hole in the tooth?
- What could Kofi have done to prevent it?

Teeth can last a lifetime if they are cared for. In this lesson we explain how plaque forms, how it leads to tooth decay and gum disease, and how to prevent both. We end with the proper way to clean the teeth.

We begin with plaque because it is the starting point of both tooth decay and gum disease.

pages.title: Plaque
pages.body:
Plaque is a soft, sticky, colourless film that forms on the teeth. It is made of bacteria, saliva and bits of food. It collects mostly between the teeth, in the grooves of the molars and along the gum line. If plaque is not removed it hardens into a rough yellow or brown layer called tartar, which only a dentist can remove.

Next we follow the steps from a sugary meal to a painful cavity.

pages.title: How tooth decay happens
pages.body:
1. Sugary and starchy food remains on the teeth after eating.
2. Bacteria in the plaque feed on the sugar and produce acid.
3. The acid slowly dissolves the enamel and makes a small hole called a cavity. There is no pain at this stage because the enamel has no nerves.
4. The cavity reaches the dentine. The tooth becomes sensitive to hot, cold and sweet foods.
5. The decay reaches the pulp cavity. Bacteria attack the nerves and blood vessels and cause severe toothache.
6. If the tooth is not treated, pus collects at the root as an abscess and the tooth may be lost.

Tooth decay is also called dental caries. Its main causes are frequent eating of sweets, biscuits and sugary drinks, poor cleaning of the teeth, and too little fluoride, which is a mineral that hardens the enamel.

Now we see how plaque also damages the gums.

pages.title: Gum disease
pages.body: When plaque and tartar collect at the gum line, the bacteria irritate the gums. The gums become red and swollen and bleed easily during brushing. This early stage is called gingivitis and it can be cured by good cleaning. If it is neglected, the infection spreads to the fibres and the bone that hold the tooth. The gums shrink away from the teeth, the breath smells bad and the teeth become loose and may fall out. This serious stage is called periodontitis.

| **Condition** | **Cause** | **Signs** | **Prevention** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plaque | Bacteria, saliva and food remains left on the teeth | A sticky film on the teeth that later hardens into tartar | Brush twice a day and clean between the teeth |
| Tooth decay | Acid made by plaque bacteria from sugar dissolves the enamel | Brown or black holes, sensitivity and toothache | Eat fewer sugary foods, brush with fluoride toothpaste and visit a dentist |
| Gum disease | Plaque and tartar at the gum line infect the gums | Red, swollen, bleeding gums, bad breath and loose teeth | Clean the gum line gently and have tartar removed by a dentist |

The good news is that both conditions can be prevented by simple habits.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Preventing tooth decay and gum disease

pages.title: Preventing tooth decay and gum disease
pages.body:
- Brush the teeth at least twice a day, in the morning and last thing at night, with fluoride toothpaste.
- Clean between the teeth with dental floss or a clean chewing stick.
- Eat fewer sweets, toffees and sugary drinks, and do not eat them between meals.
- Eat foods rich in calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D, such as milk, small fish eaten with bones and eggs, to build strong teeth.
- Eat fresh fruits and vegetables. Vitamin C keeps the gums healthy, and crisp foods such as carrots help to clean the teeth.
- Rinse the mouth with water after meals.
- Do not use the teeth to open bottles or crack hard objects.
- Visit a dentist for a check at least once a year, and at once if a tooth hurts.
To finish, we learn the steps of good brushing.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The proper way to clean the teeth

pages.title: The proper way to clean the teeth
pages.body:
1. Use a soft toothbrush and a small amount of fluoride toothpaste, about the size of a pea.
2. Hold the brush at a slant towards the gum line.
3. Brush the outer surfaces of the upper teeth downwards from the gum and the lower teeth upwards from the gum, using short gentle strokes.
4. Brush the inner surfaces of all the teeth in the same way.
5. Brush the chewing surfaces of the premolars and molars with a back and forth movement.
6. Brush the tongue gently to remove bacteria.
7. Spit out the foam. Brush for about two minutes in all.
8. Rinse the brush, keep it upright to dry and replace it about every three months.

A chewing stick, when used properly, also cleans the teeth well. Chew one end until it forms soft bristles, then use the bristles to clean every surface of each tooth.

> **Did you know?** Brushing too hard with a hard brush does not clean better. It wears away the enamel at the neck of the tooth and can injure the gums.

- A tooth has three regions. The crown is above the gum, the neck is at the gum line and the root is fixed in a socket in the jawbone.
- Enamel is the hard outer layer of the crown, dentine forms most of the tooth, the pulp cavity contains blood vessels and nerves, and cement fixes the root in its socket.
- Humans have 20 milk teeth and then 32 permanent teeth.
- Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars crush and grind food. An adult has 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars.
- Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria, saliva and food. Its bacteria change sugar to acid, which dissolves enamel and causes tooth decay.
- Plaque at the gum line causes gum disease, with red, swollen, bleeding gums and later loose teeth.
- Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, eating less sugar, eating foods rich in calcium and visiting a dentist keep the teeth and gums healthy.
